newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Moody's says new NZ govt won't affect its rating.
newsitem.headline: Moody's says new NZ govt won't affect its rating.

text.p: Moody's Investors Service said on Wednesday that the announcement of a new New Zealand government would have no material impact on its credit rating.

"The profile from our perspective continues to place the country firmly in the AA-1 rating category for its foreign currency debt and AAA for its domestic debt," Vice President, senior analyst Yves Lemay told Reuters.
"The bottom line from our perspective is we don't anticipate new players in a new government would have any material impact on the rating," he said.
"Overall, the policy thrust is still pointing in the same direction," said Lemay, speaking from New York.
"Other measures such as the postponement of the tax cuts and the establishment of a superannuation fund speaks to the maintainance of conservative and sound economic policy going forward," he said.
On Tuesday night a coalition was formed between the nationalist New Zealand First Party and the conservative caretaker National Party government.

New policies announced included postponing by a year tax cuts originally planned for 1997, conducting a referendum on the introduction of compulsory pensions, broadening the Reserve Bank's inflation target to 0-3 percent from 0-2 percent and including sustainable economic growth in the bank's targets.

Asked about the addition of the sustainable growth objective, he said: "This is not unique to New Zealand. Other countries have dual sets of objectives and still perform extremely well on the inflation front. Canada would be a good example."

Asked about new fiscal projections which show the budget surplus for the 1999/2000 fiscal year shrinking to NZ$2.7 billion from the previous forecast of $6.1 billion, he said: "From our perspective the overall budgetary position of New Zealand makes many countries quite envious when you are talking about surpluses of those magnitudes.

He said sustained significant surpluses would continue to have a positive effect on the level of national savings which in turn helped finance investment activities of the country so that it did not have to rely on external savings.

"So to the extent that these budgetary surpluses remain significant in the future that should continue to have a positive influence on national savings, investment activity and ultimately long-term growth," he said.
Lemay declined to comment on the appointment of NZ First leader Winston Peters as Treasurer.
